items.stem: A trader holds a customer limit order to buy 500 shares at $20.00 while the firm displays a bid of $19.98. The market is quiet and the order is marketable against the firm's quote. What does the limit-order display obligation generally require?

options.text: Display the customer's better-priced limit order (or route it) so it is reflected in the quote
options.rationale: Correct: a customer limit order priced better than the firm's quote must generally be displayed or routed promptly.

options.text: Hold the order hidden until the firm can trade ahead of it
options.rationale: Trading ahead of a displayable customer limit order is prohibited.

options.text: Cancel the order because it improves the firm's quote
options.rationale: Improving the quote is not a basis to cancel a customer order.

options.text: Delay display until end of day
options.rationale: Display must be prompt, not deferred to end of day.

items.explanation: Correct: a customer limit order priced better than the firm's quote must generally be displayed or routed promptly.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: During a single-stock trading pause under limit-up/limit-down, a trader wants to keep sending marketable orders. What is the correct understanding of the pause?

options.text: Trading in that security is halted for the pause period; orders cannot execute until trading resumes
options.rationale: Correct: an LULD pause halts trading in the security until the re-opening process completes.

options.text: Only customer orders are paused; proprietary orders execute normally
options.rationale: The pause applies to the security, not to a class of orders.

options.text: Orders execute but at the prior day's close
options.rationale: Executions do not occur at a stale close during the pause.

options.text: The pause only affects options on the stock
options.rationale: The pause affects trading in the underlying security.

items.explanation: Correct: an LULD pause halts trading in the security until the re-opening process completes.

items.stem: A compliance review flags a trader's activity near the close. Which TWO patterns are most consistent with prohibited manipulation rather than legitimate trading? (Select TWO)

options.text: Entering a series of small aggressive buy orders in the final seconds solely to set a higher closing print
options.rationale: Correct: trading designed to set an artificial closing price is marking-the-close manipulation.

options.text: Executing a large customer sell order worked throughout the day to minimise impact
options.rationale: Working an order to reduce impact is legitimate execution practice.

options.text: Buying ahead of a known large customer order to profit from its expected impact
options.rationale: Correct: front-running a customer order is prohibited.

options.text: Posting a displayed limit order that improves the NBBO
options.rationale: Improving the quote with a genuine order is ordinary market-making.

options.text: Reporting an executed trade within the required time window
options.rationale: Timely trade reporting is a compliance obligation, not manipulation.

items.explanation: Correct: trading designed to set an artificial closing price is marking-the-close manipulation. Correct: front-running a customer order is prohibited.
